pos: v. (archaic past participle of pluck; plucked, broken off)
etymology: An older spelling of plucked, from Old English pluccian, to pull off or pick. The -t ending preserves the sound of the clipped past participle, as in mixt, fetcht and dropt. The Hebrew taraph means freshly plucked.
biblical_def: The second dove returns to Noah with the sign the whole world had been waiting for: “And the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth” (Genesis 8:11). Pluckt is the older spelling of plucked, and the Hebrew carries the sense of freshly plucked — not a leaf found floating but one taken from a living tree. That is the whole evidence. A week earlier the same dove had found nothing: “But the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him into the ark” (Genesis 8:9). Now there is a tree above water, growing, with leaves to pluck. One leaf in a bird's beak told a man in a wooden box that the judgment was over and the earth was alive again. The flood is the standing pledge of God's sworn mercy: “For this is as the waters of Noah unto me: for as I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth; so have I sworn that I would not be wroth with thee, nor rebuke thee” (Isaiah 54:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PLUCK, to pull with sudden force or effort; to pull off, as to pluck a leaf; PLUCKT, an older form of plucked.
webster_full: PLUCK, v.t. To pull with sudden force or effort; to pull off, as to pluck feathers or fruit.
To strip by plucking; as, to pluck a fowl.
PLUCKT is an older spelling of plucked, with the clipped -t ending.

Isa 54:9
For this is as the waters of Noah unto me: for as I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth; so have I sworn that I would not be wroth with thee, nor rebuke thee.
corruption_summary: The flood is downgraded to local legend or borrowed myth, which empties the covenant sign of the leaf and the bow of its historical ground.
corruption_paragraphs: Mainstream academic treatment makes Genesis 6 to 9 a reworking of Mesopotamian flood epics, and liberal theology has long treated the narrative as mythological material carrying a moral. The dictionary holds a historical Noah and a historical worldwide flood, as the New Testament does: our Lord compares His own coming to the days of Noah, Peter grounds an argument on the eight souls saved, and Hebrews lists Noah among the men of faith.

The cost of the mythological reading is the covenant. If there was no flood, there was no ark, no leaf, no bow in the cloud, and nothing for God to swear by in Isaiah 54:9 when He pledges never to be wroth with His people. The whole comfort of that verse depends on an event in history. A freshly plucked olive leaf in a bird's beak is either the first evidence of a renewed earth or it is nothing at all.

pos: v. (archaic past tense of fetch; fetched, went and brought)
etymology: An older spelling of fetched, from Old English feccan, to bring. The clipped -t ending belongs with mixt, pluckt and dropt. The Hebrew laqach means to take or fetch.
biblical_def: When the three strangers come to Mamre, Abraham's hospitality is told in a string of hurrying verbs: “And Abraham ran unto the herd, and fetcht a calf tender and good, and gave it unto a young man; and he hasted to dress it” (Genesis 18:7). Fetcht is the old spelling of fetched, and the verse has four motions in one breath: ran, fetcht, gave, hasted. A man of great age and great wealth, with servants to spare, runs to his own herd. Nothing in the account is grudging or ceremonious; the best calf is taken, the finest meal kneaded, and the host stands by them under the tree while they eat. Only afterward is it revealed who had come. The New Testament makes this the standing argument for Christian hospitality: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Hebrews 13:2), and Paul lists it as a duty of ordinary saints: “Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality” (Romans 12:13). The haste is the point. Hospitality that must be scheduled a month out is a different thing from Abraham running to the herd.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FETCH, to go and bring; to bring from a distance; FETCHT, an older form of fetched.
webster_full: FETCH, v.t. To go and bring; to bring from a distance.
To bring; to bring back; to recall.
FETCHT is an older spelling of fetched, with the clipped -t ending.

corruption_summary: Hospitality is reduced to entertaining friends at convenience, so that the stranger at the door, which is the biblical case, is never the one received.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain shape of Genesis 18: a stranger appears, the host runs, the best is killed, and the guest is served before anyone asks who he is.

Modern hospitality has become a social category — peers invited in advance, the house prepared, the occasion mutual. Scripture's word philoxenia means love of strangers, and its examples are unannounced: three men at Mamre, two angels at Lot's gate, a prophet at a widow's door, travelling preachers lodged by Gaius. Hebrews gives the reason with a sidelong glance at Abraham's calf: some have entertained angels unawares. Four verbs in a row — ran, fetcht, gave, hasted — are the whole doctrine in practice.

pos: v. (archaic past participle of forbear; ceased, refrained, left off)
etymology: Old strong past participle of forbear, Old English forberan, to bear with, to abstain from, from for- (away) and beran (to bear). The Hebrew chadal means to cease or leave off.
biblical_def: In the oracle against Babylon the fall of her soldiers is described not as defeat in the field but as a refusal to fight: “The mighty men of Babylon have forborn to fight, they have remained in their holds: their might hath failed; they became as women: they have burned her dwellingplaces; her bars are broken” (Jeremiah 51:30). To have forborn is to have ceased or left off. The verse is a careful anatomy of collapse: the men do not lose, they decline; they keep to their strongholds; their might fails inwardly before any wall is breached. God had already pronounced the city incurable: “We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed: forsake her, and let us go every one into his own country: for her judgment reacheth unto heaven, and is lifted up even to the skies” (Jeremiah 51:9). The same verb, in its past tense forbare, describes something very different elsewhere — a prophet choosing to leave off speaking to a king who would not hear (2 Chronicles 25:16). To forbear may be courage or it may be the failure of nerve; the difference lies in what is being left off and why.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FORBEAR, to cease; to hold from proceeding; to abstain; FORBORN, the old participle, now forborne.
webster_full: FORBEAR, v.i. To stop; to cease; to hold from proceeding.
To pause; to delay; to abstain; to refrain.
FORBEAR, v.t. To avoid voluntarily; to spare; to treat with indulgence.
FORBORN is the old strong participle, now written forborne.
Jeremiah 51:30 says the mighty men of Babylon have forborn to fight.

Jer 51:9

And it came to pass, as he talked with him, that the king said unto him, Art thou made of the king's counsel? forbear; why shouldest thou be smitten? Then the prophet forbare, and said, I know that God hath determined to destroy thee, because thou hast done this, and hast not hearkened unto my counsel.
corruption_summary: Fortification is trusted as safety, so that men keep to their holds while their courage fails, and the collapse is complete before the wall is touched.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Jeremiah's anatomy of a fall: the mighty men forbore to fight and stayed in their holds, and their might had already failed inside them.

Babylon had the most formidable walls in the ancient world, and they did her no good because the men behind them had stopped fighting. Institutions fall the same way. A church, a family or a ministry may keep every structure intact — the constitution, the buildings, the schedule — while the courage to contend for the faith quietly drains out, and the collapse when it comes looks sudden only to onlookers. Walls are not nerve, and the holds men trust in are no stronger than the men who hold them.

pos: v. (archaic past tense of forbear; refrained, held back, spared)
etymology: Old strong past tense of forbear, Old English forberan, on the pattern of bear/bare. The Hebrew chadal means to cease; in Jeremiah 41:8 it carries the sense of sparing.
biblical_def: After the murder of Gedaliah, Ishmael spares ten men because of what they could offer him: “But ten men were found among them that said unto Ishmael, Slay us not: for we have treasures in the field, of wheat, and of barley, and of oil, and of honey. So he forbare, and slew them not among their brethren” (Jeremiah 41:8). To forbear is to refrain or spare, and this is a forbearance of the basest kind: a murderer stays his hand for grain and honey. The same verb in the same tense describes something nobler in Amaziah's court, where the prophet is told to be silent and complies, but not before delivering the sentence: “Then the prophet forbare, and said, I know that God hath determined to destroy thee” (2 Chronicles 25:16). Two men forbear; one spares out of greed, one falls silent out of obedience and leaves the king to the judgment he has chosen. And the Christian use of the word is a third thing entirely: “Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye” (Colossians 3:13).

webster_full: FORBEAR, v.i. To stop; to cease; to abstain; to refrain.

Col 3:13

corruption_summary: Restraint is praised without regard to its motive, so that a cruelty paused for profit is counted in the same column as a patience exercised for Christ's sake.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that forbearance is not a virtue in itself; its worth lies entirely in its motive. Ishmael forbare, and he was no better for it — he spared ten lives for wheat, barley, oil and honey, having butchered the rest.

The modern habit of praising moderation as such makes this distinction hard to see. A man who does less evil than he might is congratulated; a company that harms fewer people than it could is called responsible. Scripture measures otherwise. The prophet before Amaziah forbare in obedience and still spoke the word of judgment; Christian forbearance in Colossians 3:13 is patterned on Christ's forgiveness of us. Restraint for gain is only calculation. Restraint for the sake of another is grace.

pos: v./adj. (archaic form of mixed; mingled, of blended origin)
etymology: An older spelling of mixed, from Latin mixtus, past participle of miscere, to mingle; the -t is in fact closer to the Latin. The Hebrew asaphsuph in Numbers 11:4 means a collected rabble, a gathering of mixed people.
biblical_def: The murmuring in the wilderness is traced to a particular source: “And the mixt multitude that was among them fell a lusting: and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, Who shall give us flesh to eat?” (Numbers 11:4). Mixt is the older spelling of mixed, and the mixt multitude is the rabble of non-covenant people who had come up out of Egypt with Israel. The order of the verse is deliberate: the lusting began among them, and the children of Israel wept also. Discontent spread from the fringe into the camp. Nehemiah records the eventual remedy when the law was read in Jerusalem: “Now it came to pass, when they had heard the law, that they separated from Israel all the mixed multitude” (Nehemiah 13:3). The principle is not ethnic, for Ruth the Moabitess and Rahab of Jericho were received into Israel by faith and are in the line of Christ. The issue is covenant: “Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you” (2 Corinthians 6:17).

webster_full: MIX, v.t. To unite or blend promiscuously, as substances or bodies.

corruption_summary: The mixt multitude is read as a warrant for ethnic exclusion, or else the call to separation is dismissed as tribalism; both miss that the line Scripture draws is covenantal.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors stand on either side. Some have used these texts to support racial separation, which Scripture flatly refuses: Rahab the Canaanite and Ruth the Moabitess were received into Israel by faith and both stand in the genealogy of Christ, and in the gospel there is neither Greek nor Jew but all one in Him. Any reading of Numbers 11 that justifies exclusion by blood is a corruption of the text.

The opposite error, far more common now, treats the whole category of separation as tribal anxiety and calls the church to a boundaryless inclusion. Paul will not have it. Come out from among them, be ye separate, touch not the unclean thing is apostolic command, and it concerns covenant and conduct, not ancestry. The mixt multitude was dangerous because it was in the camp without being in the covenant, and the first thing it produced was an appetite the camp could not satisfy.

pos: v. (archaic past participle of shape; formed, fashioned)
etymology: Old strong past participle of shape, Old English scieppan, to create or form, the same root behind -ship in words like worship. The Hebrew chul means to be brought forth or travailed with.
biblical_def: In the greatest of the penitential psalms David traces his adultery back past the act to his nature: “Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psalm 51:5). Shapen is the old participle of shape, and the confession is not that David's conception was sinful nor that his mother sinned in bearing him, but that he was formed from the beginning in a nature already fallen. He is not excusing himself; he is going deeper than excuse. The psalm has just asked for mercy according to God's lovingkindness, and the next verse asks for a cleansing no man can perform: “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 51:7). Paul states the doctrine as history: “as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned” (Romans 5:12). This is original sin, imputed from Adam and inherent in every child of his; and Psalm 51 is the proof that a right confession of it does not drive a man to despair but to the only hyssop that cleanses.

webster_full: SHAPE, v.t. To form or create; to mould or make into a particular form.

corruption_summary: Original sin is denied, so that children are held to be born morally neutral and sin becomes a behaviour learned rather than a nature inherited.
corruption_paragraphs: Pelagianism in the fifth century taught that men are born innocent and sin only by imitation; semi-Pelagianism softened it; modern evangelicalism very often assumes it without naming it, speaking of an age of accountability and treating children as neutral until they choose. Progressive theology goes further and treats the doctrine of original sin itself as a harmful teaching about human nature.

Scripture is explicit and the confessions follow it. David traces his sin to his formation, Paul traces death to one man's transgression imputed to all, and Ephesians calls us by nature children of wrath. The doctrine is not cruelty but diagnosis, and everything depends on it: a patient misdiagnosed as neutral needs only instruction, while a patient shapen in iniquity needs a new birth. That is why Psalm 51:5 stands two verses from a plea to be purged with hyssop and made whiter than snow.

etymology: Past tense of spit, Old English spittan, of imitative origin. The Greek ptuo is likewise imitative. Mark uses the related form spit in his parallel healings.
biblical_def: The healing of the man born blind begins with the most undignified act in the Gospels: “When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay” (John 9:6). The Creator stoops, spat, mixes earth with His own spittle and puts it on a man's eyes. The echo of Genesis is unmistakable: the hands that formed Adam of the dust of the ground form eyes of clay for a man who had never had sight. And the cure required obedience before it gave light: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing” (John 9:7). Mark records the same method with another man: “And he took the blind man by the hand, and led him out of the town; and when he had spit on his eyes, and put his hands upon him, he asked him if he saw ought” (Mark 8:23). The Lord who received spitting in His face at His trial gave sight by His own spittle. Nothing in the incarnation is too lowly for Him to use.

corruption_summary: The physical means in Christ's healings are either read as folk magic or spiritualised away, when they display the dignity of His true humanity and the sovereignty of His method.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings miss this verse from opposite sides. Comparative-religion treatments file the clay and spittle with ancient healing magic, as though Christ were employing a technique whose power lay in the materials. And a certain docetic squeamishness in the church, uncomfortable with so bodily an act from the Son of God, hurries past the spittle to the lesson.

Both lose the doctrine. Chalcedonian Christology holds one Person in two natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion or division; the spittle is the Son of God's own, and it heals because of who He is, not because of what it is. He healed elsewhere by a word at a distance, which forecloses any magic in the mud. And the method preaches: the Maker of Adam from dust makes eyes from clay, sends the man to the pool called Sent, and gives light through obedience.

pos: v. (to trim, to cut away the edge or surface of; here, to trim the nails)
etymology: From Old French parer, to adorn or trim, from Latin parare, to prepare. To pare is to cut away the outer part. The Hebrew asah, to do or make, is here used of dressing the nails.
biblical_def: The law governing a woman taken captive in war requires a month of transition before any marriage: “Then thou shalt bring her home to thine house; and she shall shave her head, and pare her nails” (Deuteronomy 21:12). To pare is to trim, and these acts — shaved head, trimmed nails, the raiment of captivity laid aside — mark a formal break with the woman's former life and the beginning of a protected standing in Israel. The statute addresses a real and brutal situation: “And seest among the captives a beautiful woman, and hast a desire unto her, that thou wouldest have her to thy wife” (Deuteronomy 21:11). It does not license the desire; it constrains it severely. “And she shall put the raiment of her captivity from off her, and shall remain in thine house, and bewail her father and her mother a full month: and after that thou shalt go in unto her, and be her husband, and she shall be thy wife” (Deuteronomy 21:13). A full month of mourning, in his house, untouched; then marriage with the standing of a wife, and the following verse forbids selling her if he later has no delight in her.

webster_full: PARE, v.t. To cut off, as the superficial substance or extremities of a thing.

corruption_summary: The captive-wife statute is cited as divine permission for wartime rape, when the law was given to forbid precisely that and to give the woman the standing of a wife.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 21:10-14 is among the most frequently misrepresented passages in Scripture, offered as proof that the God of Israel licensed the sexual use of captives. The dictionary rejects the charge on the ground of what the statute actually requires, clause by clause.

Every provision runs against the soldier's impulse. He may not touch her: she is brought to his house, her hair shaved, her nails pared, the clothes of her captivity removed, and she mourns her father and mother a full month. Only then may he marry her, and the marriage makes her a wife, not a slave or a concubine. If he afterwards has no delight in her he must let her go free and may not sell her, and the text gives the reason: because he hath humbled her. In the ancient world of total war, where captive women had no standing whatever, this law stands almost alone in protecting one. It restrains lust, imposes delay and grief, and forbids disposal.
roots_summary: Latin parare, to prepare, through Old French parer, to trim; Deuteronomy 21:12 has the captive woman pare her nails.

pos: v. (past tense; unloosed the girding or harness of, unburdened)
etymology: From un- and gird, Old English gyrdan, to encircle or bind. To ungird a camel is to loose its harness and lift its load. The Hebrew pathach means to open or loose.
biblical_def: Abraham's servant, arriving at Nahor with ten camels and a mission, is received in a verse full of ordinary kindness: “And the man came into the house: and he ungirded his camels, and gave straw and provender for the camels, and water to wash his feet, and the men's feet that were with him” (Genesis 24:32). To ungird a camel is to loose its harness and set down its burden. Four things are done in that one verse, and three of them are for the animals before anything is done for the men. This is the hospitality of a household that had not yet heard the errand. The servant himself refuses to be served until he has spoken: “And there was set meat before him to eat: but he said, I will not eat, until I have told mine errand. And he said, Speak on” (Genesis 24:33). The whole chapter is a sustained lesson in providence received with prayer, and the servant's own confession names it: “Blessed be the LORD God of my master Abraham, who hath not left destitute my master of his mercy and his truth: I being in the way, the LORD led me” (Genesis 24:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): UNGIRD, to loose from a girdle or band; to unbind; GIRD, to bind by surrounding with any flexible substance.
webster_full: UNGIRD, v.t. To loose from a girdle or band; to unbind.
GIRD, v.t. To bind by surrounding with any flexible substance, as a band or girdle.
To invest; to furnish; as, to gird with strength.
Hebrew pathach, to open or loose.
Genesis 24:32 says he ungirded his camels, and gave straw and provender.
scriptures: And the man came into the house: and he ungirded his camels, and gave straw and provender for the camels, and water to wash his feet, and the men's feet that were with him.
And there was set meat before him to eat: but he said, I will not eat, until I have told mine errand. And he said, Speak on.
And he said, Blessed be the LORD God of my master Abraham, who hath not left destitute my master of his mercy and his truth: I being in the way, the LORD led me to the house of my master's brethren.
corruption_summary: The ordinary duties of care — for beasts, for travellers, for a guest's tired feet — are treated as beneath notice, when Scripture records them as the texture of a godly house.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Genesis 24 spends a verse on unloading camels and feeding them straw, and that the Holy Spirit thought the detail worth preserving.

A religion of large gestures finds such verses tedious. But Scripture repeatedly honours the small duty done well: a righteous man regardeth the life of his beast; the ox is not to be muzzled in the treading; a cup of cold water given to a little one is noticed. The house at Nahor loosed the harnesses, fed the animals, and brought water for the feet of men whose business they did not yet know. That is what hospitality looks like when nobody is watching, and it is the setting in which the servant's prayer was answered.
roots_summary: Un- plus gird, Old English gyrdan; Hebrew pathach, to loose; Genesis 24:32 has the camels ungirded at Nahor.
roots_lines: Old English gyrdan, to encircle or bind, gives gird and ungird.
Hebrew pathach, to open or loose.
Genesis 24:32 is the only occurrence of ungirded in the Authorized Version.
Three of the four acts in the verse are for the animals.
The servant refused to eat until he had told his errand.
usage: he ungirded his camels, and gave straw and provender

pos: adj. (fragrant; of a pleasing odour, said of an acceptable sacrifice)
etymology: A compound of sweet, Old English swete, and smelling. The Greek is euodia, a sweet smell, from eu (well) and ozo (to smell), the same word used of the Philippians' gift.
biblical_def: Paul sets the whole Christian walk under the pattern of Christ's self-offering: “And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour” (Ephesians 5:2). Sweetsmelling renders euodia, and the phrase is drawn straight out of Leviticus, where the burnt offering is “an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD” (Leviticus 1:9). The point is Godward. Christ's death is not described here primarily by its effect on us but by its acceptability to the Father: it ascended as the smoke of a whole burnt offering, received with delight. And the command that frames it is imitation: “Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children” (Ephesians 5:1). Believers are to walk in love as Christ also hath loved us — which in context means self-giving, not sentiment, since the model is a man on a cross. The same Greek word describes the Philippians' money sent to a prisoner, an odour of a sweet smell, acceptable and well-pleasing to God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SWEET-SMELLING, having a sweet smell; fragrant; SAVOR, scent; odor; that which renders a thing acceptable.
webster_full: SWEET-SMELLING, a. Having a sweet smell; fragrant.
SAVOR, n. Taste or odor; scent; smell.
A sweet savor, in Scripture, denotes that which is acceptable to God.
Greek euodia, a sweet smell, from eu, well, and ozo, to smell.
Ephesians 5:2 calls Christ's self-offering a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour.
scriptures: Eph 5:2
And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour.
Eph 5:1
Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children;
Lev 1:9
But his inwards and his legs shall he wash in water: and the priest shall burn all on the altar, to be a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD.
corruption_summary: The cross is described only in terms of its effect on us, so that its Godward direction as an accepted sacrifice is lost and the atonement becomes a demonstration rather than an offering.
corruption_paragraphs: Moral-influence and exemplarist accounts of the atonement, from Abelard to modern progressive evangelical writers who reject penal substitution, describe the cross as God's demonstration of solidarity and love, affecting us rather than propitiating Him. The language of sacrifice is retained as metaphor and the direction is reversed: nothing is actually offered to the Father.

Ephesians 5:2 will not permit the reversal. Christ gave Himself to God, as an offering and a sacrifice, for a sweetsmelling savour — the exact phrase Leviticus uses of the whole burnt offering ascending from the altar. The cross is first a transaction with the Father, in which the Son's obedience unto death is received with delight, and only therefore the demonstration of love that the same verse calls us to imitate. Lose the Godward offering and the love has nothing to demonstrate; keep it, and the believer's self-giving walk has an altar to stand on.
roots_summary: Sweet plus smelling; Greek euodia; Ephesians 5:2 calls Christ's self-offering a sacrifice for a sweetsmelling savour.
roots_lines: Old English swete, sweet, compounded with smelling.
Greek euodia, a sweet smell, from eu, well, and ozo, to smell.
Ephesians 5:2 is the only occurrence of sweetsmelling in the Authorized Version.
The phrase is drawn from the burnt offering of Leviticus 1:9.
The same Greek word describes the Philippians' gift to Paul in prison.
usage: an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour
names the Godward acceptability of Christ's self-offering
